steps.user_message: I'm going through a legal process and need to organize my thoughts. The case involves contract dispute with a former employer. My lawyer is Michael Torres at Dowd Legal; we have proceedings at family court in Denver. The judge set a status conference in two months.. Opposing party: the respondent in the case. This is in Fulton County, Georgia. My status has changed and I need to understand the implications. Can you help me figure out what to ask my attorney about how to protect my interests in the settlement talks? I want to be ready for the legal next steps.
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with legal-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
I can help — this is a good time to get organized. Before I make specific suggestions, two quick clarifying questions because some details conflict:

- You say the proceedings are “at family court in Denver” and also “Fulton County, Georgia.” Which court (city/state) is the matter actually in?  
- What exactly changed about your status? (e.g., you were served, you filed an answer, you lost/accepted a settlement offer, changed residence/employment, had a scheduling order entered, etc.)

Once you confirm that, here’s a practical checklist of things to prepare and focused questions to ask Michael Torres so you protect your interests in settlement talks and are ready for the status conference.

1) What to clarify with your lawyer (high-priority questions)
- Case status & schedule
  - What is the exact timeline/deadlines now (status conference date, discovery cutoffs, dispositive motion deadlines, trial date if any)?
  - What will happen at the status conference and what should I expect to say or submit?
  - Are there immediate deadlines I must meet before the conference?

- Settlement authority & strategy
  - What are our primary settlement objectives? (money, confidentiality, non-disparagement, career protections, clearing records, etc.)
  - What is my BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) and my walk-away/minimum acceptable terms?
  - Do you recommend mediation or another form of ADR before the conference?
  - Who on the other side has authority to settle? Do we have confirmation they can approve our requested terms?

- Terms and protections to insist on
  - How should the release be written so it’s narrow (only releases specified claims) rather than excessively broad? What language do you recommend?
  - Should we include a non-admission clause (“no admission of liability”)?
  - Confidentiality and public filings: can settlement terms be kept confidential? If not, how can we minimize exposure?
  - Non-disparagement: do we include it, and how broadly worded should it be?
  - Will the settlement affect any other proceedings or claims (e.g., unemployment, administrative claims, other courts)?

- Payment and enforcement
  - What payment structure protects me best (lump sum at signing vs installment with security/escrow)?
  - If payments are installment, what security can we require (escrow, promissory note, confession of judgment, personal guarantee)?
  - What remedies do we include if they breach (liquidated damages, attorneys’ fees, expedited relief)?

- Legal and practical consequences
  - Tax consequences of the settlement (is any portion taxable compensation vs. damages?) — should I consult a tax advisor before agreeing?
  - Will I be required to return anything or sign non-compete/non-solicit clauses? If so, how enforceable are they?
  - Will the settlement bar me from pursuing related claims in other forums (carve-outs/exceptions)?
  - Will the settlement require court approval or affect any orders the judge must enter?

- Costs and fees
  - Who pays attorneys’ fees and costs? Can we include recovery of fees if respondent breaches?
  - What will you estimate our remaining litigation costs and your fees to the status conference/trial if we don’t settle?

2) Documents and facts to bring to your meeting
- Copy of the employment/contract at issue (all versions, amendments)
- Any severance agreements, prior settlement offers, or release drafts
- All relevant communications (emails, texts, letters) between you and the former employer/respondent
- Pleadings filed by either side, court orders, the judge’s scheduling order
- Timeline of events (dates of key incidents, termination, offers)
- Financial records showing damages/loss of earnings (pay stubs, W-2s, bank records)
- Any witnesses’ contact info and summaries of what they will say

3) Specific settlement-protection clauses to request or review carefully
- Precise Release language (define claims released and exclude unrelated claims)
- Non-admission of liability clause
- Confidentiality clause with narrowly defined exceptions (counsel, tax advisor, court order)
- Non-disparagement clause (mutual if possible) with clear definitions
- Payment terms, security (escrow, certified funds), deadlines, and default remedies
- Enforcement clause: venue/jurisdiction for enforcement, attorneys’ fees for enforcement
- Carve-outs (e.g., preservation of right to file with government agencies, worker’s comp, or to disclose to spouse/attorney/tax professional)
- Dismissal language: who will file the dismissal and when; with or without prejudice
- Retention of jurisdiction by the court (if helpful for enforcement)

4) Practical negotiation items and strategy to discuss with counsel
- Prioritize must-haves vs. nice-to-haves (list 3 non-negotiables)
- Contingency for the offer (how long it’s open; whether it’s revocable)
- Staged negotiation plan: initial demand, likely counter, walk-away point
- Whether to use a neutral mediator or private settlement conference
- Communication protocol (who handles direct contact with the respondent or counsel)

5) Preparing for the status conference
- Ask Michael what the court will want to know about settlement efforts and whether the judge will encourage/require mediation
- Whether a joint status report or proposed scheduling order should be filed in advance
- Whether you should appear (in-person/telephonic) or if counsel will appear only
- What the judge’s likely expectations are regarding discovery readiness and readiness to set dates

6) Additional professional checks
- Ask Michael whether you should consult a tax advisor about settlement allocation (employer-related payments may have different tax treatment)
- If confidentiality/non-compete matters arise, consider an employment-law specialist opinion if Michael is not specialized

7) Example short script / email you can send to Michael (I can draft this for you)
“Michael — I want to be fully prepared for the status conference in two months and for settlement talks. Can we discuss: (1) the exact schedule and what will happen at the status conference; (2) our settlement objectives and BATNA; (3) recommended protective clauses (release scope, payment security, confidentiality, non-disparagement); (4) tax consequences and whether I should consult a tax expert; and (5) what documents you need from me now. Also, please advise what I should say at the status conference and whether I need to file anything beforehand. Thanks — [Your name]”

If you want, I can:
- Draft that email to Michael Torres for you now (I would send it if you tell me to).  
- Convert the checklist into a one-page handout you can take to your meeting.  
- Tailor the questions if you confirm which court (Denver vs Fulton County) and explain what the status change was.

Which of the follow-up options do you want me to do next?
